en: An Excerpt from the Preface to the Sub-commentary on the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha:
Alas! Human life is like a dream; every passing moment is empty. Wealth and honor are equal to drifting clouds; fame and achievement are like the morning dew.
The affections of one’s youth suddenly vanish into the burial mounds; the splendor of the mundane world swiftly returns to the hands of woodcutters and herdsmen. This being so—

Vast and boundless is the sea of karmic retribution; all are submerged in the mud of hell and *niraya*. Endless is the realm of the underworld; it is difficult to evade the stern countenances of the spectral hosts.

When vengeful spirits face interrogation, the mountains of knives and trees of swords are no mere idle talk. As one undergoes rebirth according to one’s karma, the wombs of horses and donkeys are all considered evil destinies.
Only the Buddha Amitābha of the Western Land has made great vows and given rise to compassion.
The mind leads sentient beings to join in the joyful play of the Pure Land. Boundless light pervades everywhere; inconceivable merits provide its adornment.
Jeweled nets beautify the sky, and jade forests line the paths. The gold and green of the towers and terraces shine brightly;

the precious ground is radiant and glorious, reflecting the blue and yellow of the pond waters. The lotuses are fragrant and pure, the music is resonant and clear, and flowers fall in profusion as the Dharma is proclaimed.
The harmonious and elegant sounds of birds are none other than the Buddha-dharma; listening to their resonant melodies is itself the aspiration for the Way.
This is the site of practice for pure karma and the power of Amitābha’s vows. Those born in this land who single-mindedly hold the Name shall all ascend to the other shore through the nine grades;
those who pity others and extinguish their offenses shall likewise realize non-arising through ten recitations.

To be welcomed by the Buddha of Transformation is superior to practicing the Way through other gates. It is like a sail catching a favorable current, reaching the harbor of benefit with swift progress;
it is like a stone placed upon a great ship, avoiding sinking into the sea of suffering. With such expediency, do not hesitate for a moment.
(Huaiting) My hair is dyed with the frost of age, and I grieve that the day is drawing to its close. I am deeply afraid of being reborn as a beast with fur and horns; I seek only to be rescued.
There is no other way. Desiring to seek liberation from defilement and detachment from the dust of the world, one must apply oneself with vigor to spiritual cultivation.

A single scroll of the Amitābha Sūtra is a compassionate vessel for crossing over; a thousand recitations of the Buddha’s name can open the path to enlightenment. Greed, anger, and ignorance, along with all prior evils, are difficult to eliminate even over kalpas of time.

By faithfully upholding the vows from this day forward, the provisions for the journey will be complete. I hereby respectfully declare my long-held aspiration and venture to inform those of like mind.
Recorded respectfully by the lay practitioner (upāsaka) Xu Huaiting of Lèjìng, aged sixty-nine, on the second month of the year Dīngmǎo in the sixth year of the Tóngzhì era.
Preface.
This sutra is the power of Amitābha’s vows, extolled by Śākyamuni. Within its preceding and succeeding sections, there are naturally subtle threads to be followed.
Following the example of Prince Zhaoming of the Liang Dynasty’s division of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, I have established twelve divisions.
Each division is given a specific title, and the essential meaning of each is annotated below, analyzed in detail and categorized for clarity. Open [the gates of understanding].
The scroll is clearly divided;

this sutra is read in four major sections. The first section provides a general overview of both the environment (*niśraya*) and the inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhāna*). (Section Two) First, it clarifies the environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).

(Sections Three, Four, and Five) Next, it clarifies the retribution of the inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*). (Section Six) It concludes with fourfold adornments, referring to them as the "Land of Bliss."

This is its supreme excellence. The second section concerns rebirth. It first speaks of those who have already been born [in that land] (the seventh division), and next speaks of those who have not yet been born (the eighth division), concluding with the aspiration to be born there; thus it states that one should aspire to be born there.

The third section concerns the scriptural text itself. It first speaks of the universal praise of all Buddhas (the ninth division), and next speaks of the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas (the tenth division).
This concludes with the sealing [of the teaching] through faith, acceptance, and the making of vows, stating that upon hearing this sutra, one ought to give rise to faith. This is the fourth section.
In the "Mutual Praise of the Buddhas" (the eleventh division), difficult matters are praised by the Buddhas to encourage deep faith;

it serves as a summary of the entire sutra, stating that sentient beings ought to sever doubt and give rise to faith, thereby responding to and repaying the Buddha’s kindness. Upon hearing [this], one must certainly make a vow; the vow must necessarily [precede...]
Faith. Exhorting and guiding layer by layer with a heart of pure compassion, one investigates with meticulous care; its meaning is inexhaustible.

This sutra takes the Buddha-lands as its standard, faith and aspiration as its entrance, the holding of the name as its actual practice, rebirth in the Pure Land as its verification, and the scriptural text as its teaching. Circles are used to mark the key points of application.
□ is used for the entrance; ○, a continuous circle, is used for the place of actual practice; ◎, a double circle, is used for the place of realization;
丶丶, two dots, are used for the place of signs and responses; △, a continuous triangle, is used for the place of the teaching, to clarify the eyebrows and eyes.
The *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* (*Mìtō Shūchão*) is a work by the Great Master Lianchi to advocate for the Pure Land and uphold the True Dharma.
It is extensively cited and broadly referenced, with evidence presented in meticulous detail, totaling over one hundred thousand words;
it is the most comprehensive and exhaustive of its kind. I have extracted its essence and annotated each phrase of the sūtra text below, making it easy to consult, and have titled it:
This is titled *An Excerpt from the Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra*. May readers not forget Master Yunqi’s supreme intention to bestow grace upon future students.
Recorded respectfully by the Layman Lejing. Section One:
The Assembly of Witnesses at the Dharma-Assembly. Section Two: The Primary and Secondary Features of the Buddha-Land.
Chapter Three: The Jewel Trees and Lotus Pools; Chapter Four: Offerings from the Gods and Humans; Chapter Five:
Birds and Trees Proclaiming the Dharma; Chapter Six: The Immeasurable Virtues of the Buddha;
Chapter Seven: Aspiration for Rebirth; Chapter Eight: Cultivating Right Practice.
Chapter Nine: Mutual Praise and Exhortation to Faith; Chapter Ten: Hearing the Dharma and the Aspiration for Faith;
Chapter Eleven: Mutual Praise and Arousing of Sentiment; Chapter Twelve: Universal Propagation and Universal Salvation.
An Excerpt from the Sub-commentary on the Buddha-spoken *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Commentary by the Great Master Yunqi Lianchi.
Compiled by the Pure Practice Disciple Xu Huaiting.
"The Buddha" refers to our own Teacher, Śākyamuni. It was this Śākyamuni Buddha of this land who spoke of him...
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Scripture on Amitābha Buddha) is a scripture concerning the adornments of the land and its inhabitants, as well as rebirth through faith and aspiration.
The original title of this scripture was the *Sūtra of the Praise of the Inconceivable Merit Admired and Protected by All Buddhas*;
the current title was established by Master Kumārajīva.
Chapter One: The Section on the Witnesses of the Assembly.
This belongs to the Introductory Section (*nidāna*). "The assembly" refers to the gathering for the preaching of the Dharma. "Witnesses of the assembly" refers to those who collectively bear witness.
1. The assembly of Śrāvakas. 2. The assembly of Bodhisattvas. 3. The assembly of devas and humans.
Thus have I heard. "Thus" (*evam*) is a term signifying faith and compliance. "I" (*aham*) refers to Ānanda himself. "Heard" (*śrutam*) indicates that he personally heard it from the Buddha.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: At the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he instructed Ānanda, saying: "At the beginning of all sūtras, one should say..."
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in a certain country, at a certain place; this is in accordance with the Buddha’s own instruction.
At one time the Buddha was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī;
this is the time when he preached the sutra. The Buddha is Śākyamuni. The kingdom of Śrāvastī is [the capital of] King Prasenajit.
The place where the King resided was the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Jeta was the crown prince of King Ajātaśatru; the trees were planted by Jeta’s own hand, while the king’s minister, Sudatta...
Nā. He provided relief to the poor and was known as the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Deeply revering the Buddha-dharma, he purchased a grove from Jeta, covering the ground with gold, and consequently built a vihāra to invite the Buddha to preach the Dharma.
"Together with the great community of bhikṣus" means to be in their company. There are three meanings of "bhikṣu": first, a mendicant; second, one who terrifies Māra; third, one who destroys evil.
"Great" refers to the profundity of their attainment of the Way. "Saṃgha" means the assembly.
Together with one thousand two hundred and fifty people:
the three Kāśyapas—first, Uruvilvākāśyapa, who had five hundred disciples; second, Gayākāśyapa, who had three hundred disciples;
and third, Nadīkāśyapa, who had two hundred disciples—as well as Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra, these two together...
Two hundred and fifty disciples all came to take refuge in the Buddha, together completing this number. "Together" (俱) carries the meaning of being combined with the aforementioned group.
All of them were great Arhats.
From the first fruit to the fourth fruit, all are stages of the śrāvaka; these are the four fruits. There are three meanings of arhat:

first, "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat), for one whose pure conduct is established and who, by principle, should receive offerings; second, "Slayer of Thieves" (Arahan), for one who has already severed the afflictions of thought and completely extinguished the turbulent flow [of defilements];
third, "Non-arising" (Anāgāmin), for one whose conditions for birth are exhausted and who will not undergo further existence. By means of...
Possessing wisdom but lacking compassion, he does not come into the dusty world to teach and deliver sentient beings; therefore, he is called a "Han who delivers himself alone.
He is well-known to all, of lofty virtue and great reputation, his fame filling the world, known and recognized by everyone alike.

The Elder Śāriputra: "Elder" (*sthavira*) is a title for one of long-standing virtue and seniority. This applies to the sixteen venerable elders who follow below. *Śāri* means "pigeon" (*śārika*), and *putra* means "son.
Because his mother’s eyes were as clear as those of a pigeon, he was named after her. At the age of eight, he ascended the seat to deliberate.
In debate, he was peerless. Within seven days, he attained a thorough mastery of the Buddha’s teachings; thus, he was foremost in wisdom.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana: *Mahā* means "Great.
*Maudgalyāyana* means "of the clan of Mung beans"; his surname was Kauṣṭhila. His personal name was Kolita.
He is called "Great" to distinguish him from his kinsmen. When the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, a venomous dragon obstructed him;
Maudgalyāyana manifested various large and small forms, and the dragon, struck with fear, finally submitted. Thus, he is foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

Mahākāśyapa—here translated as "Great Kauruṣya"—is his clan name; his personal name is Pipphala, though he is also called "Drinking Light. There are three types of Kāśyapas, and he is designated as "Great" (Mahā) to distinguish him from them.
Although Kāśyapa was advanced in years, he did not abandon the dhūta practices, for which the Buddha deeply praised his possession of them.

Regarding the practice of *dhūta*: thus, he was foremost among those who practice *dhūta*. According to records, when the World-Honored One was at the assembly on Vulture Peak, he held up a flower to show the multitude;
only Kāśyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye;
I entrust it secretly to you. Thereupon, he was transmitted as the First Patriarch.

Mahākātyāyana—this is translated as "Ornamented" (Wénshì)—was his clan name. He belonged to the Brahmin caste of South India. He was skilled in discerning meanings and extensively expounding the path of the teachings;
therefore, he was foremost in formal debate and exposition.

Mahākauṣṭhila—translated here as "Great Thigh"—was so named after his physical appearance. He was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra. Through diligent and zealous effort, he attained the four types of analytical eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*);
thus, he was able to answer any question posed to him, and for this reason, he was foremost in answering questions.

Revata, which means "constellation" (nakṣatra) in this language, was born from a star-worshipper who prayed for a son. Because his mind is upright, he is free from inversion; because his mind is concentrated, he is not distracted.
Therefore, he is foremost among those who are free from error and confusion.
Cūḍapanthaka, which is translated here as "Successor on the Path.
His mother gave birth to him while traveling along the road; he was so named because he could continue [the journey] on the path.

Having entered the monastic life, he was dull-witted and remained for a long time without understanding anything. The Buddha had him recite the two characters "broom" (sammajjani). He would remember one and forget the other, and so it continued for a long time.
He suddenly attained awakening; with defilements exhausted and delusions removed, he became an Arhat.
Nanda—translated as "Good Joy"—has three [namesakes]: Ānanda, Sundarananda, and this one.
This is Nanda the Cowherd. Ānanda means "Joy of Celebration" (Qingxi) in this language.
He was the Buddha’s maternal cousin, born on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment; because the entire nation rejoiced at his birth, he was so named.
Name: Ānanda. He attended the Buddha for twenty-five years and did not forget a single word of the Dharma the Buddha taught;
thus, he was foremost among those of great learning. Kāśyapa transmitted the Dharma to Ānanda, who became the Second Patriarch.
Rāhula is translated here as "Obstructing" (Fùzhàng). He is so named because he was able to use his hand to shield the sun and moon; he is the son of the Buddha.
Because he accumulated meritorious practices while remaining unknown to others, he is foremost in secret conduct.
Gavāmpati—translated here as "The Cow-Chewer"—received this name because he was afflicted by an illness resulting from his having mocked śramaṇas in a past life.
He constantly dwelt in the heavens where the devas venerated him; thus, he was foremost among those who received celestial offerings.
Pindolabharadvāja: the first three characters mean "Immovable," which is his name; the last three characters mean "Sharp Faculties," which is his clan name.
Placing the name before the clan name serves to distinguish him from others.
Kālodāyin—this is translated as "Black Radiance" (Heiguang). His complexion was a beautiful black, yet it was radiant. Mahākapphiṇa.

This is called the lunar mansion *Bharaṇī*. He was born under the propitiation of the star *Bharaṇī*. Without relying on the astronomical instruments of the *ji* and *heng*, he thoroughly understood celestial phenomena;
thus it is known that he was foremost among those who know the stars. Bakula.
This one is named Shanrong (Good Appearance). His countenance is upright and handsome. In the past, he observed the precept against killing for ninety-one kalpas;
consequently, his life was never cut short prematurely, and he reached the age of one hundred and sixty. For this reason, his longevity is foremost.
Aniruddha—this is translated as "Free from Poverty.
In a past age of famine, he once offered millet porridge to a Pratyekabuddha. For ninety-one kalpas, his resources were sufficient and abundant.
Later, having left the household life, he was fond of sleep; when the Buddha preached the Dharma, he fell into a deep slumber and did not wake. The Buddha rebuked him.
He reproached himself and applied himself with such fervent diligence that his eyes did not close for a single blink; consequently, he lost both his physical eyes.
Through the Buddhist practice of the *Ratnaprabhāsa-vajrasamādhi*, he subsequently attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and thus became foremost among those with divine vision.
Such are these great disciples. Thus the section is concluded.
By this same principle, the others are to be understood. "Great disciples" refers to the great bhikṣus, the great arhats.

Together with the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they received the preceding words as the Buddha spoke this sutra. It was not only the śrāvakas who were present in the assembly; the great beings likewise heard it together.
"Bodhisattva" is translated here as "Awakened Being" (Jue Youqing); "Mahāsattva" refers to a great bodhisattva among bodhisattvas.
Mañjuśrī Dharma-rāja-putra—also called Mañjuśrī, which in this language means "Wondrous Auspiciousness.

At the time of his birth, light filled the room, and various auspicious signs appeared, such as an elephant with six tusks. The Buddha is the Dharma King; the Bodhisattva has entered the correct stage of the Dharma.
He is named Dharmaputra (Son of the Dharma).
The Bodhisattva Ajita—here translated as "Invincible"—is none other than the Bodhisattva Maitreya. Maitreya is a clan name here translated as "The Benevolent One" (Maitri).
"Ajita" is his name. Because he possessed a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) even while in his mother’s womb, he was named after that lineage.
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that he made a vow to protect sentient beings during the *kalpa* of weapons;
thus, his loving-kindness flourishes in this world and his compassion reaches the future eons. Therefore, none can surpass him.
The Bodhisattva Gandhahasti; this is translated as "Unceasing.
He practices all pure conducts (*brahmacarya*) throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, never resting for a moment.
[He is] the Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent.
For the sake of even a single sentient being, they have long transformed them without receiving [their gratitude], never for a single moment abandoning them;
thus, together with such great bodhisattvas, they form a group,
and the remaining cases are the same as before.
Śakra Devānām-Indra and others followed the preceding discourse on the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land. Not only were the various sages assembled there, but all the ordinary beings heard it as well.
Śakra Devānām-Indra means "The Lord of the Gods"; he is Śakra (Indra). After the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha...
At that time, a woman conceived the aspiration to construct a stūpa, and thirty-two people assisted her.

Because the present King [Śakra] rules over the thirty-two heavens of the four directions in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, he is called the Lord of Devas (*devendra*). The term "and so forth" refers to these thirty-two [deities], as well as others.
"Accompanied by an immeasurable multitude of devas.
"Immeasurable devas" refers to those who govern the heavens of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. "A multitude" refers to the various devas who have descended.
"Human beings and asuras" refers exhaustively to the sentient beings of the six realms of existence. The word "together with" (俱) connects back to the preceding text;
above it was said, "together with a great assembly of bhikṣus," while here it says, "together with a great assembly of bodhisattvas and devas."
Section Two: The Distinction Between the Environment and the Embodiment of the Buddha-land.

This section provides a general demonstration of the two types of retribution—the environment and the embodiment—and serves as the structural outline for the entire sutra. The "land" (kṣetra) is that which is relied upon and is thus termed "retributive environment" (*niśraya-vipāka*).

The "Buddha" is that which relies [upon the land] and is thus termed "primary embodiment" (*mukhya-vipāka*). First, by designating the land, the environment is revealed; second, by designating the Lord, the primary embodiment is revealed.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Śāriputra.
The phrase "the Buddha addressed" means that the Buddha spoke of himself. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the white tuft of hair emits light, inaugurating the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
When Vimalakīrti manifested illness in Vaiśālī, he expounded the discourse on non-duality;

in the *Perfect Enlightenment*, the *Vajra*, and other sutras, the Buddha generally first received a question before subsequently proclaiming and expounding the teaching. This present sutra is not so.

This is truly because the sentient beings of the final age have dull faculties and deep obstructions, making liberation extremely difficult to attain. Out of great compassion, the Buddha has brought forth this [sutra].

This gate cuts across birth and death and urgently rescues sentient beings; fearing only that it may not reach them in time, it is therefore proclaimed spontaneously without waiting for an invitation.
It is addressed solely to Śāriputra because he is foremost in wisdom.
"To the west of here, passing through ten billion Buddha-lands, there is a world named Sukhāvatī.
This indicates the land and reveals its basis. "Here" refers to this realm. Both Saha and Sukhāvatī are located within the thirteenth layer of the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpasaṃbhava*).
Regarding the relationship between these two lands, "passing" means proceeding from here toward the west, extending horizontally across.
Beyond that lies a great trichiliocosm, which is called a single Buddha-field. From this Sahā world, one must pass through ten trillion such Buddha-fields to reach it;
how far removed it is! Yet the *Contemplation Sūtra* states that Amitābha’s land is not far from here.
This is because when pure karma has been perfected, the mind at the moment of death while abiding in meditative concentration is itself the mind that receives rebirth in the Pure Land.
One attains rebirth in a single thought-moment; there is no need to worry about the distance. "Ultimate Bliss" (Gokuraku) is also called "Peaceful Bliss" (Anraku) and "Peaceful Nurturing" (An'yō).
There are four kinds of Ultimate Bliss: first, the Land of Constant Dharma-nature Light (Jōjakukōdo). As the sutra says: "Vairocana pervades all places;
the dwelling place of that Buddha is named Constant Dharma-nature Light. This is the abode of those who have attained the ultimate fruit. Second, the Land of True Reward...
1. The Land of Adornment (*vyūha-bhūmi*): By practicing the true Dharma, one receives a sublime retribution adorned with the seven treasures;

this is the dwelling place of Mahāsattvas of the Dharmakāya. 2. The Land of Skillful Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*): Having severed the delusions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsa-kleśa*), it belongs to the Path of Skillful Means;

because ignorance (*avidyā*) is not yet exhausted, it is called "with remainder. This is the dwelling place of the noble ones of the Three Vehicles. 3. The Land of Co-residence of Ordinary Beings and Sages (*prthagjana-ārya-sahavāsa-bhūmi*).

This is a realm where the four classes of noble ones and the six realms of ordinary beings dwell together. Since it is now said that there is a great assembly of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and devas, this is a land of shared dwelling.
In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha.
This heading indicates the primary subject and clarifies the correct [teaching]. The characters follow from above:

since every land must have a master, the text points to the master who resides therein as the Buddha, specifically citing the name of the Original Buddha as Amitābha. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "In a past kalpa..."
There was a wheel-turning monarch named A-raṇa-smṛti (Vimalacitta). He made this vow, saying: "I shall practice the Mahāyāna and take hold of a pure land;
I will never aspire to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a defiled land.
May the sentient beings of that world be free from all suffering and affliction. If I do not obtain such a buddha-field, I shall not achieve perfect enlightenment. Now, this has indeed been realized.
He is named Amitābha; therefore, he manifests the Pure Land. Furthermore, the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra] states:
"The Bhikṣu Dharmākara, in the presence of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, conceived the unsurpassed aspiration and extensively proclaimed forty-eight vows. If it were not so..."
"I vow not to attain Buddhahood. At that time, the earth shook violently and the heavens rained down exquisite flowers. From the air, voices raised in unison, praising him, saying:
"You shall certainly attain Buddhahood;
you now preach the Dharma in the present."
The Buddha delivers all sentient beings; the method by which he delivers them is called "preaching the Dharma. The *Mahāmegha Sūtra* states:
"At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with a serene countenance, and from his face issued immeasurable light.

He declared that in the western world there is a land named Sukhāvatī, where the Buddha is titled Amitāyus, who currently dwells and preaches the Dharma. This refers precisely to the preaching of Śākyamuni.
At that time, Amitābha was also preaching the Dharma there; therefore, it is said that he "currently preaches the Dharma.

The section from the third phrase onward, beginning with "jeweled trees and lotus ponds," clarifies the adornments of the *niśraya* (the environment). This describes the excellence of the light and flowers upon both land and water in the world of Sukhāvatī.
...Thus it is. First, a general indication; second, the rows of trees; third, the jewel ponds; fourth, the terraces and pavilions; fifth, the lotus flowers; finally, a summary.
Śāriputra, for what reason is that land called "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī)?
This explains the land upon which [the teaching] relies. That land is named Sukhāvatī (Utmost Bliss), which differs from the Sahā world; it should be described in detail so that joy may arise.
The sentient beings in that country have no manifold sufferings, but experience only various forms of bliss; therefore, it is called Utmost Bliss.

First, a general summary; second, a detailed analysis. Regarding the various sufferings: the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates in their fullness—these are called the eight sufferings.

However, because those beings in that land are born by transformation within lotus flowers, they lack the suffering of birth. Because cold and heat do not shift [there], they lack the suffering of old age. Their bodies are free from...
By being free from the segmentation of the body, there is no suffering of illness; by having immeasurable life-span, there is no suffering of death;
by having no parents, wife, or children, there is no suffering of separation from the beloved; by dwelling together with those of supreme goodness, there is no suffering of encountering the hated;

by having all that is desired arrive of its own accord, there is no suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; and by contemplating emptiness and illuminating stillness, there is no suffering of the five aggregates’ proliferation. These are the various joys.
This refers to what is explained in the subsequent section.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, regarding the Land of Ultimate Bliss—
this following passage clarifies the matters of bliss therein.
There are seven layers of railings;
those that run horizontally are called *lan* (crossbars), and those that run vertically are called *shun* (balusters). These railings encircle the exterior of the tree.
There are also seven layers of netting.
A net covers the trees. The *Mahāvaipulya* (Daben) states: "The net is soft and supple, like *tūla* cotton. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (*Guānjīng*) states:
"A net of exquisite pearls completely covers the trees; each tree has seven layers of nets, and within each interstice of the nets, there are five hundred billion palaces of exquisite flowers."
There are seven rows of trees.
As for "rows of trees," it means they are formed in successive lines. The *Mahāvaipulya* states:

"Upon the various jeweled embankments, there are countless sandalwood trees and auspicious fruit trees, arranged in rows facing one another; these constitute 'rows of trees. Regarding the 'sevenfold': first..."
There are layers of railings surrounding a single row of trees; these layers alternate with one another, numbering seven in total.
All are composed of the four precious substances and encircle [the area] on every side.
The four treasures are gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Regarding that which "surrounds them on all sides," the *Śrī-sampad-vyūha-sūtra* states:
"Immeasurable jeweled nets, all adorned and embellished with golden threads, pearls, and hundreds of thousands of various gems, are draped on all four sides with golden bells.
Their radiance and colors are brilliant and magnificent, spreading over and covering the trees. The same applies to the railings, which are likewise adorned with jewels.
This can be understood. Furthermore, the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra] states: "The various trees made of the seven treasures fill the world.

Those with golden roots and golden stems, where the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all gold, are called 'single-treasure' trees. Those with golden roots and silver stems, where the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are likewise divided between gold and silver, are called 'two-treasure' trees.
In this manner, there are three-treasure, four-treasure, and so on, up to seven-treasure trees. This corresponds to what is said here.
The four treasures are somewhat unique;
for this reason, that land is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī).
This concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the land of Ultimate Bliss there are ponds made of the seven treasures.
Following from what was said above, it is not only the adornments of the dry land that are magnificent; even the waters of the ponds are likewise supreme and wondrous.

The *Mahāsukhāvativyūha* (The Great Sutra) states: "On the inner and outer sides, to the left and right, there are various bathing pools, like a great ocean, composed of the seven treasures. It further says:
Some pools are made of gold; some are made of silver; some are made of crystal and lapis lazuli; some are made of coral and amber;
and so on, up to pools made of the seven treasures. The seven treasures are described below.
The water of eight virtues fills its interior:

first, it is limpid and pure; second, it is cool and refreshing; third, it is sweet and delicious; fourth, it is light and soft; fifth, it is moistening and lustrous; sixth, it is tranquil and harmonious;
seventh, it removes hunger and thirst; eighth, it nourishes and develops the sense faculties. Possessing these eight kinds of virtue, it benefits all sentient beings.
The bottom of the pond is entirely covered with ground of golden sand.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states: "The channels are made of pure gold; beneath the channels, the bottom sand consists of various colored diamonds.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "The golden ponds have silver sand at their bottoms; the crystal ponds have lapis lazuli sand at their bottoms. (2)
The ponds are made of jewels; their bottoms consist of two types of sand, and so on up to the seven precious substances, which are likewise the same.
Here, only "golden sand" is mentioned for the sake of brevity.
The steps and walkways on the four sides are composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
This refers to the area outside the pond. Regarding the "four sides": the center is the pond water, while the surrounding four sides consist of stairways and paths.
A "stairway" (kai) is that which rises above the ground; a "path" (dō) is a level thoroughfare. These are composed of the four treasures, such as gold and silver.
Above are pavilions and towers, likewise adorned with the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, mother-of-pearl, red pearl, and agate.

A multi-storied building is called a *lou* (pavilion); a high, peaked tower is called a *ge* (tower). These are the seven treasures, such as gold and silver. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "Yellow..."

Upon the golden ground, within each and every jewel, there are five hundred colored rays of light. These rays are like flowers, forming luminous terraces and tens of millions of multi-storied pavilions composed of a hundred treasures.
The *Mūla-sūtra* states: "The lecture halls and monasteries of Amitābha Buddha [are thus adorned]."
The palaces and towers are all made of the seven treasures; those in which the bodhisattvas dwell are likewise so.
The palaces and towers of the devas and humans correspond to their respective forms and colors, varying in height, depth, and size, and are composed of either one or two treasures.
It reaches immeasurable jewels. The *Avataṃsaka* says: "Perilous towers wind around it; galleries extend out from the sides. Roof beams and structures support one another;
windows and doors reflect each other. The steps, courtyards, balconies, and pillars are all fully provided with every variety, and everything is adorned with the seven treasures."
The lotuses in the pond are as large as chariot wheels;
this refers to their size within the pond. The term "chariot wheel" describes their shape. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states:

"In each pond there are lotuses made of the seven treasures, perfectly round and twelve *yojanas* in circumference. The *Mahāsukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states: "Lotuses of various jewels, surrounding [the ponds]..."
Pervading the entire world, each jewel-flower has immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of petals; thus one may know the vastness of these flowers.
The *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* states: "At that time, the World-Honored One was sitting upright at the site of enlightenment within the multi-storied sandalwood pavilion."
He manifested a supernatural transformation: there appeared thousand-petaled lotuses as large as chariot wheels, within which were emanated Buddhas,
each emitting hundreds of thousands of rays of light— blue light from blue forms, yellow light from yellow forms, red light from red forms, and white light from white forms.

Regarding the mention of their "colors," it is not merely that the colors are cited; rather, the term "radiance" (*ābhā*) is used because the lotus flowers of that land are supremely pure and thus possess radiance.
The *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra] states: "Blue flowers have blue radiance; white flowers have white radiance;
and for the colors of azure, yellow, vermilion, and purple, their radiances are likewise so. Blazing, brilliant, and resplendent, they outshine the sun and moon. Within each and every flower..."
He emitted three trillion six hundred billion rays of light. From within each ray of light, there emerged three trillion six hundred billion Buddhas.

Each of these Buddhas, in turn, manifested hundreds of thousands of further rays of light, which universally preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the sake of sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
This mention of "four colors" is a textual abbreviation.

"Subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure" describes its virtues. It is "subtle" because it is composed of the seven treasures; "wondrous" because it is miraculously born from the emanations of all Buddhas;
"fragrant" because it is clear, fresh, and serene; and "pure" because its substance rests upon golden sand. The lotus flowers of that land differ from those of this world. (6)
Sentient beings who aspire to be born in the Pure Land will, in the mere twinkling of an eye, be born by transformation within a lotus flower.

As stated in the following passage, "If one maintains a single-minded focus without distraction, one shall immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss," this means that one is born within such a lotus flower.
Those who practice the Pure Land path, when reciting the Buddha’s name, should constantly visualize themselves seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) within a lotus flower. The Buddha...
He will receive me within a lotus flower. Thereafter, one should single-mindedly hold the Name.

In the past, there were two monks who visualized the opening and closing of a lotus flower and thereby attained rebirth there; how much more so for those who further add single-minded recitation of the Name—there has never been one who did not attain birth.
Śāriputra, the land of Ultimate Bliss is adorned with such meritorious accomplishments.
The draped lattices, rows of trees, ponds, pavilions, and lotus flowers—all these various adornments are accomplished through the merit of Amitābha Buddha.
Aspiration and practice constitute merit; the perfection of that merit constitutes accomplishment.
The Vows of Dharmākara state: "When I become a Buddha, those born in my land shall all be born by transformation from lotus flowers within ponds of the seven treasures.

It further states: "When I become a Buddha, from the ground upward to the very limits of space within my land, there shall be palaces and towers, as well as ponds, streams, flowers, and trees, all fashioned from immeasurable varieties of precious jewels, numbering in the hundreds of thousands."
Various incenses were combined together. Now, having come to attain Buddhahood, all his vows have been fully accomplished.
Section Four: The Supreme Offerings of Gods and Humans in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
This refers to the excellence of the offerings made by gods and humans in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Part One: Celestial Music; Part Two: Gold.
1. The ground; 2. The rain of flowers; 3. Making offerings to the Buddha; 4. Returning to the country; 5. Personal enjoyment; at the end, a general summary.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in that buddha-land, celestial music is constantly played.

This refers to celestial music. The *Mahāvaipulya* states: "First, the gods of the Four Heavenly Kings and various other devas offer hundreds of thousands of fragrant flowers and hundreds of thousands of musical instruments as offerings to the Buddha, as well as to the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas."

Thereupon, from the second Trāyastriṃśa Heaven King and the various devas of the desire realm, up to the seventh Brahmā Heaven, all the devas presented incense, flowers, and music, each succeeding one being twice as magnificent as the last. As the *Sūtra on Contemplation* states: "Immeasurable devas perform celestial music;
furthermore, there are musical instruments suspended in the void like precious celestial banners, which resonate spontaneously without being struck."
When people of today recite the Buddha’s name, on the day of their passing, celestial music welcomes them into the void; this is precisely because the Pure Land constantly produces celestial music,
and its ground is made of gold.

This follows the previous section to introduce the subsequent one. Regarding the "ground of golden hue": it is not only that one hears celestial music with the ears, but one also beholds celestial flowers with the eyes.
As for the "golden" [hue], it refers to the ground of lapis lazuli interspersed with gold. The *Amitābha-sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"One sees the lapis lazuli ground, transparent and radiant both within and without; beneath it are diamond pillars made of the seven treasures and gold, supporting the lapis lazuli ground."
Above, it was bound with golden cords interspersed and interlaced; according to this, the golden [cords] constitute the adornment of the lapis lazuli ground.
Six times throughout the day and night, it rains celestial *mandārava* flowers.
This refers to the golden ground where celestial flowers rain down constantly. Six periods constitute the day and six periods constitute the night, forming one full day.
*Mandāra* is the name for a celestial flower; it is a white flower. The *Mahāvastu* states: "All the devas..."
They all brought hundreds of thousands of celestial flowers and incenses to make offerings to that Buddha, as well as to the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.

Furthermore, Subhūti, you have eloquently explained the Prajñāpāramitā; Śakra scattered flowers because he knew that those who are reborn in the Pure Land maintain a single-minded state without distraction.
Thus, no discursive thoughts arise, and the myriad dharmas are empty and quiescent—this is indeed what it means to "eloquently explain."
Prajñā, how could you have any doubt regarding the response of the devas?

The sentient beings of that land always, at the break of dawn, each take a robe-sack filled with various exquisite flowers to make offerings to hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas in other directions.
This refers to the flowers rained down from heaven, which sentient beings gather to offer to the Buddha.

"Sentient beings" here includes all those from the Bodhisattvas who descend [to this world] down to ordinary people at the stage of initial resolve who are reborn in that land. "Early morning" refers to the clear and pure atmosphere of dawn.
"Constantly" means it is always so day after day; "each" means it is thus for every individual. "Cloth satchels" refers to those used to carry flowers.
"Vessel" (器) refers to either a bowl or the lapel of a robe. "Other lands" (他方) means going from one's own country to another country.

"Ten million *koṭi* Buddhas" means that for each Buddha there is a great trichiliocosm; this expresses their vastness and distance. Regarding "making offerings," the *Mūla-sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:

"All bodhisattvas, sustained by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, in the time it takes to eat a single meal, travel everywhere to immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions to make offerings to all [the Buddhas]."
The Buddha [is honored with] flowers, incense, music, robes, canopies, banners, and pennants—countless articles of offering.
If one wishes to present flowers, they transform in mid-air into flower canopies, all of which incline downward to constitute an act of worship.

At the very time for eating—that is, at the hour of the morning meal, when dawn breaks into the morning fast—the time is extremely brief; it is by means of this most minimal interval of time that he returns to his own country.
Making offerings to the greatest number of Buddhas demonstrates his swiftness. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Da ben) states:
"Having completed the offerings, he suddenly rose up lightly and returned to his own country, even before the meal had been eaten."
Regarding "eating and walking":
since the preceding section discussed the time of eating, this next passage speaks of eating; it refers to the self-comfort experienced after a meal. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"For those who are reborn there, at the time of eating, silver bowls and golden bowls appear before them according to their wishes, filled with food and drink of a hundred flavors."
It filled them completely; whether sour, salty, sweet, or bland, each was according to their wishes. Once eaten, it vanished of its own accord, leaving no residue.
Some saw its color or smelled its fragrance and took this as food, becoming naturally satiated and comfortable. When the meal was finished, it dissolved away; when the time came, it appeared again.
As they passed through, the cycle continued without interruption. Having eaten, they would walk about, strolling at their ease.

Śāriputra, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is adorned with such meritorious adornments as the celestial music and the rain of flowers mentioned above; all these various adornments are accomplished through the merit of Amitābha Buddha.
As stated in the vows of Dharmākara: "When I become a Buddha, the bodhisattvas within my land shall [offer] incense and flowers..."
With various such offerings, when he wishes to travel to other world-systems to make offerings to the Buddhas, he can reach them all in the time it takes to eat a single meal. It is further said:

"When I become a Buddha, whenever those in my land wish to eat, food and drink of a hundred flavors shall manifest before them within precious bowls. Now that I have attained Buddhahood, all my vows have been fully realized."
Chapter Five: The Attainment of the Birds and Trees Preaching the Dharma.
This section describes the excellence of the Dharma-hearing experienced by sentient beings in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Part One: The Transformation Birds Preach the Dharma.
Second, the winds and trees proclaim the Dharma; this concludes the final summary.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that land constantly possesses various wonderful birds of diverse colors.
From here below, it speaks of the transformation-birds proclaiming the Dharma. "Various" means not being of one kind; "wonderful" means extraordinary; "diverse" [means...]
"Form" refers to what is beautiful to behold:
the white crane, the peacock, the parrot, the śāri bird, the kalaviṅka, and the *saṃjīva* (conjoined-life) bird.
These are mentioned as one or two examples from among many varieties. The white crane, the peacock, and the parrot are all found in this land.
"Venerable. *Śāri* refers to the śārika bird; *kalaviṅka* means "wonderful voice" (*miao yin*). Even before emerging from its shell, it already possesses a melodic sound.
*Saṃjīva* refers to a single body with two heads; this is the two-headed bird found on the Snowy Mountains.
These various birds produce harmonious and elegant sounds during the six periods of day and night.

The birds of that land produce their voices throughout the day and night; they are "harmonious" (he) because they are gentle, supple, and balanced, and they are "elegant" (ya) because they are grand, upright, and solemn.
That sound expounds and clarifies the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).

"Expound" means to unfold and expand; "clarify" means to make thorough and penetrating. The five faculties are: first, faith; second, diligence; third, mindfulness; fourth, concentration; and fifth, wisdom.
These are called "faculties" because they are able to produce the noble path.
The five powers (pañcabala) are the aforementioned five faculties (pañcendriya) when they have increased and possess great strength.
The seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyanga).
These are the seven factors of enlightenment: first, investigation of phenomena; second, energy; third, joy; fourth, tranquility; fifth, equanimity; sixth, concentration; and seventh, mindfulness.
They are applied according to their respective capacities.
[Then there are] the eightfold noble path.
It is also called the Eightfold Noble Path: first, right view; second, right intention; third, right speech; fourth, right action; fifth, right livelihood; sixth, right effort;
seventh, right mindfulness; and eighth, right concentration. It is called "right" because it does not rely on partiality or deviation, and it is called a "path" because it can lead to nirvana.
Regarding such dharmas as these—
the twenty-five chapters above, as well as all other remaining dharmas—
when the sentient beings of that land hear this sound, they all recollect the Buddha, recollect the Dharma, and recollect the Sangha.

The various Buddhas represented by carving, casting, molding, and painting—namely the *sādhāraṇa-kāya* and the *viśeṣa-kāya*—are the Buddha Jewel; the yellow scrolls and red volumes—namely the teachings, practices, principles, and fruits—are the Dharma Jewel;

and the five groups of bhikṣus—namely the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sainthood—are the Sangha Jewel. That birds are able to preach the Dharma so as to cause listeners to fix their mindfulness upon the Three Jewels clearly demonstrates their excellence.
Śāriputra, do not think that these birds are actually born as a result of karmic retribution for their sins.

You might fear that the presence of animals in the Pure Land would contradict the original vows of the Dharmakara [Bodhisattva], wondering how such creatures could exist there. Therefore, I speak of them once more.
Why is this so? Because in that Buddha-land, there are no three evil realms. To clarify the meaning of the above:
those who are obscured by the darkness of ignorance are born into the realm of animals; those who are stingy, greedy, and envious are born into the realm of hungry ghosts;
and those who commit the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes are born into the realm of hell—these are called the three evil realms. The Vows of Dharmākara state: "When I become..."

At that time, within the Buddha-field, there were no hungry ghosts or animals, nor even the smallest crawling insects; this clarifies that in that land, the evil realms did not exist from the very beginning.
Śāriputra, in that Buddha-land, even the name of the evil realms does not exist, let alone their actual presence.
Regarding the three evil realms: in that land, they are not merely unseen by the eye; they are likewise unheard of by the ear.

The very names of the three evils have never existed there, let alone their actual reality. As the Vow of Dharmākara states: "In my Buddha-land, its inhabitants shall never even hear the name of what is unwholesome, much less experience its reality. This is precisely what is meant.
These various birds are all transformations produced by Amitābha Buddha, intended to cause the sound of the Dharma to flow forth.

Since there are no evil realms there, why do those white cranes and other such creatures come to that land? It is truly because the Buddha desires the sound of the Dharma to pervade everywhere without exception;
he does not rely solely on humans to preach the Dharma, but causes the voices of these birds to all be able to preach the Dharma as well. There is no place where this is not so.
There is no time when they are not heard or perceived; this is a transformation produced by great supernatural power (*mahā-rddhi*) and is not truly existent.
As the *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "The King of Wish-Fulfilling Jewels emits a subtle, golden light, which transforms into birds of a hundred jewel-like colors.
This refers to that very phenomenon.
Śāriputra, in that buddha-land, when a gentle breeze stirs the rows of jewel-trees and the jeweled nets, they produce a subtle and wondrous sound,
like the simultaneous performance of hundreds of thousands kinds of music.
This describes the wind-trees performing the Dharma. "Wind" refers to the subtle sound, and "subtle" refers to the wondrous; it is the ultimate in beauty.
The rows of trees and their lattices are all made of the seven treasures. When struck by a gentle breeze, they strike against one another, naturally producing a subtle and wondrous sound.
It is as if the six musical scales harmonize and the eight musical tones are perfectly tuned—an ultimate state of refined elegance. Such is its sound.
It should also be understood that he extensively expounds upon dharmas such as the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment; the omission of these terms is for the sake of brevity.
Those who hear this sound will spontaneously give rise to the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha.
In the sutra, it merely mentions "wondrous sounds," yet its underlying intent includes the sound of the Dharma being preached.

If these were not the sounds of the Dharma, how could they cause people to fix their mindfulness upon the Triple Gem? The *Mahāvaipulya* states: "A gentle breeze stirs, blowing through the various jewel trees;
some produce musical sounds, while others produce the sounds of the Dharma. This is the proof.
Śāriputra, that buddha-field is adorned with such meritorious accomplishments.
The array of birds, trees, and winds described above—all these various adornments are accomplished through the merit of Amitābha Buddha.
As stated in the Vows of Dharmākara: "When I become a buddha, the people in my land shall, according to their aspirations..."

Whatever one wishes to hear, one naturally hears it. Furthermore, it is said: "By having faith, reverence, and respect for the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one now comes to attain Buddhahood, and all one's vows are fully accomplished."
The Sixth Section on the Immeasurable Qualities of the Buddha, Part One:
The preceding section clarified the adornment of the *parinirmita-vaibhoga* (environmental retribution); this section clarifies the adornment of the *sambhogika-kāya* (primary retribution).
It is said that Amitābha Buddha is accomplished through ten thousand virtues. 1. First, immeasurable radiance. 2. Second, immeasurable lifespan. 3. Third, the accomplishment of the Way.
Immeasurable. Fourth, the immeasurability of the transformed attendants. This concludes the summary.
Śāriputra, what do you think? For what reason is that Buddha named Amitābha?
This is the Buddha of this Land of the Lord of Sages. His name is Amitābha; its meaning is vast and great, and it should be expounded so as to inspire longing and aspiration.
Śāriputra, the light of that Buddha is immeasurable.
This refers to the immeasurable radiance. There are two kinds of radiance: the self-enjoyment body, which illuminates the true dharma-realm and is called the light of wisdom;
and the other-enjoyment body, which shines universally upon the great assembly and is called the light of the body. Furthermore, there is the constant radiance.
The light that is constantly manifested is neither emitted nor unemitted, such as the circular halo extending one fathom [around the Buddha].
As for those who emit light, it may be emitted from between the eyebrows, from the crown of the head, from the mouth, the teeth, the navel, the feet, and so forth. The *Mahāvaipulya* states:
"At that time, Amitābha Buddha emitted immeasurable light from his face. It further says: "By means of my wisdom..."
Light. It shines extensively throughout boundless realms, illuminating the lands of the ten directions.
The light from the crowns of the heads of the Buddhas of the ten directions reaches as far as two million worlds; only that of Amitābha...
The Buddha’s light illuminates thousands of millions of worlds without end;

therefore, he is titled the Buddha of Immeasurable Light, the Buddha of Boundless Light, the Buddha of Unobstructed Light, and so forth, up to the Buddha who Surpasses the Sun and Moon. The *Amitābha Sūtra* states:
"That Buddha possesses eighty-four thousand primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and each mark has eighty-four thousand secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*). Each sign..."

There are eighty-four thousand rays of light that shine universally upon sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha throughout the ten directions, gathering them in and never abandoning them without obstruction.
Although the sun possesses light, it still encounters hindrances; only the light of the Buddha penetrates the profound and reaches into the dark, such that nothing can obstruct it.
It refers to being obstructed and hindered by barriers. For example, there was an old woman named Sudatta who did not wish to see the Buddha; she avoided him by retreating into her inner chambers.

Yet, wherever the Buddha’s light reached, walls and enclosures were completely permeated, so that she remained constantly facing the Buddha from all four directions, both inside and out. This is the meaning.
For this reason, he is named Amitābha.
The title "Amitābha" is due to his radiance.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, as for that Buddha’s lifespan:
This refers to an immeasurable lifespan. Throughout the course of lifespans, there are both long and short durations. At this present *kṣaya-kalpa*, the lifespan is but one hundred years;

even during the *vivarta-kalpa* when it increases, it only reaches eighty thousand years. Even for universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), the Lord of Devas, or the various Buddhas who dwell in the world, their stay has a finite limit.
Only the lifespan of that Buddha is exceedingly remote, not confined by ordinary numerical measures.
As for its inhabitants:
the Buddha is the Dharma King. Those born in that land rely upon the Buddha and study the Buddha; thus they possess the significance of being "people.

With single-minded purity, they are born through transformation from lotus flowers, unlike the physical bodies subject to obstruction, which undergo aging, illness, and death; therefore, they possess a life span.
"Immeasurable and boundless asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
"Asaṃkhyeya" means "innumerable"; "kalpa" means "world-age. Doubling that [number] makes it "immeasurable and boundless."
It is said that both the Buddha and the people have immeasurable lifespans;
therefore, he is named Amitābha.
Furthermore, the name "Amitā" is derived from this lifespan.
Śāriputra, since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed until now.

This phrase "ten kalpas" signifies that his realization of the Way is immeasurable. One great kalpa consists of four phases—formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness—each lasting twenty small kalpas.
Eighty *kalpas* complete constitute one great *kalpa* (*mahākalpa*). Ten such kalpas make up ten great kalpas. Amitābha Buddha is the Buddha realized by Dharmākara.
Prior to his attainment of Buddhahood, during his stage as a bodhisattva on the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), there were not only the single cause of Dharmākara, but many other causes as well.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states, at the time of the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, there were sixteen kings.
The son left the household life and purely cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*). The ninth prince attained Buddhahood in the western direction;
that prince is none other than the present Amitābha Buddha. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (or *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) states:
"Innumerable kalpas ago, there was a universal monarch named Aśoka-smṛti (No-Contention-Thought). At that time, the king made a vow to become a Buddha in a world-system to the west. That king...
This person is none other than the present Amitābha Buddha. The *Tri-saṃdhāraṇī Sūtra* states:
"In the time of the Tathāgata Vimalajvālābhyudgatarāja, there was a bhikṣu named Viśuddhanāman who held all sūtras in his memory and extensively expounded the Dharma. That bhikṣu..."
This is none other than the present Amitābha Buddha. The *Sūtra of the Four Holy Kalpas* states:
During the time of the Tathāgata Cloud-Thunder-Roar, there was a prince named Pure Merit Rewarding All Sounds who made offerings to that Buddha. That prince is the present Amitābha Buddha.
During the time of the Golden Dragon Resolving Light Buddha, there was a Dharma Master named Immeasurable Jewel Sound. His power...
He who extensively propagated the Dharma was none other than the present Buddha Amitābha. The *Six Sūtras on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddhas* states:

"During the time of King of Emptiness Buddha (Śūnyarāja), there were four bhikṣus whose minds were shrouded by afflictions. [The Buddha] taught them in mid-air to practice the contemplation of the Buddha."
He subsequently attained the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi). That third bhikṣu is none other than the present Amitābha Buddha.

The *Saptāpramāṇa-mudrā-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* states: During the time of the Tathāgata Siṃhavikrīḍita-golden-light, there was a king named Jayasena who honored and made offerings to that Buddha and practiced the cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). That king is the present Amitābha.
This refers to Amitābha Buddha. The *Aṣṭa-ekānta-prasūta-bodhisattva-sūtra* states: "In the past, Amitābha Buddha was a crown prince.
Having heard this subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate, he upheld it with diligent application; for seven thousand years, his side did not touch his mat."
Furthermore, he converted eight thousand *koṭi-nayuta* of people, causing them to attain the stage of non-retrogression.
That prince is none other than the present Buddha Amitābha; his many eons and manifold causes must likewise be immeasurable.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that Buddha has immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are arhats,
beyond what can be known through calculation.
This statement refers to the immeasurable number of transformation-companions (*nirmāṇa-sabhāga*). Those who attain awakening through the sound of the teachings are called *śrāvaka* (Hearers).
Including the previous three fruits, the term "Arhat" refers to the fourth fruit. The phrase "not calculable" indicates their great multitude.

Name. Even those who do not aspire to be born in the heavens yet hear the name of the Buddha—know that hearing the name of the Buddha is no small or easy matter.

"Non-retrogression. This means that by hearing this sutra and hearing of the Buddha, all shall attain non-retrogression; thus, they need not wait for rebirth in that land.
Therefore, Śāriputra, you and all others should faithfully accept my words, as well as what has been spoken by all the Buddhas.
This is the third exhortation. The previous statement—that by holding the Name one attains birth [in the Pure Land]—was intended as an exhortation to form a vow.

The recipient shall not forget. The Buddhas of the six directions have already exhorted one to believe in this sutra; now, he speaks again with explicit words, saying that one must believe my words.
This is truly because [the attainment of] blessings does not arise from lack of faith, and if there is no faith, there is no way for practice to arise.
Therefore, in this sutra, the Buddha repeatedly exhorts belief. What the Buddhas have spoken is that which all Buddhas together praise and exhort others to believe.
Thus it was said.

All these people shall attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Regarding that land, the phrase "whether already born, now being born, or to be born" means that by making this vow, one will immediately attain birth there.

"Now vowed and being born now" refers to the time when the Buddha is currently dwelling in the world.
One should make this vow for one's future birth. From the time after hearing this sutra until the day of that future birth,

Only through non-arising can one come to know that the power of aspiration is thus vast and great; how could one not believe it? How could one not aspire to it?
Therefore, with faith and aspiration, the preceding text is brought to its conclusion.

First, all Buddhas were praised; second, after the Buddhas had praised [the teaching], at the conclusion the difficult matters are summarized, urging deep faith in that which is difficult to believe, thereby gathering together the essential purport of the entire sutra.
Śāriputra, just as I now extol the inconceivable merit of all Buddhas, these words have already extolled all Buddhas.
By saying "all Buddhas" rather than "Amitābha," Amitābha is included therein.
When it says "all Buddhas" below, this refers to both Amitābha and all other Buddhas, collectively extolling Śākyamuni.
Those Buddhas likewise praise my inconceivable merit, saying: "This refers to the Buddhas praising themselves.

Is this not indeed the most essential Dharma-gate for transcending birth and escaping death?
"Śākyamuni Buddha is able to perform deeds that are most difficult and rare"—this and what follows are the words of the various Buddhas.

This is the name of our Original Teacher Buddha. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "In a past kalpa, there was a great minister named Ratnasāgara who vowed to bring sentient beings to maturity in a defiled land;

In sum, these two objections are resolved by the fact that only the Buddha practices this way. Truly, among the sages and worthies of past and present, there is none who can equal him;

The "five turbidities of the evil world.

hence they are called "turbidities" (*kaṣāya*). The term "evil world" refers to the world as perceived by Śākyamuni.

Regarding the *kalpa-kṣaya* (the turbidity of the eon): when the human lifespan decreases to twenty thousand years, one enters the *kalpa-kṣaya*. During the time of Śākyamuni’s world, the human lifespan was one hundred years;
having long endured this turbid age, within this very turbidity, the various defilements converged, resulting in confusion and disorderly mixture; hence it is called "turbidity."

The turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*): Once the sense faculties and their objects have come into contact, suffering and pleasure follow one upon another, and various views become agitated and chaotic, thoroughly confusing the true nature; hence it is called "turbidity. This is the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).

furthermore, it is as brief as foam, bubbles, or a lamp in the wind. Hence, it is called "turbid."
To attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—this is called the foremost and most difficult task.

In this world of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), human beings are born; externally they are oppressed and distressed by the currents of time and circumstance, and internally they are entangled by the obstructions of delusion.
This is all the more so for those whose bodies belong to the four modes of birth and whose lives depend upon [the conditions of existence].
Breathing in and out, those who desire purity become defiled; those who seek to ascend instead fall.

Yet within this very state, one may forever sever ignorance and transcend the three realms to attain unsurpassed *bodhi*. Thus, while others remain in the burning house, one alone drives the precious chariot.
While [others] were drowning together in the river of craving, you have ascended in excellence to the other shore; this is the inconceivable merit of self-benefit.
For the sake of all sentient beings, you preach this Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe.
This refers to the second set of difficult challenges. There are ten points briefly cited regarding this dharma that is difficult to believe.
First, dwelling now in this defiled land, one hears of the pure and magnificent adornments of that land and doubts that such a thing exists.

Second, even if one believes in that land, one further doubts that rebirth in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is necessarily required, given that one could be reborn in any of the Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions. Even if one were to believe...
First, there is doubt as to how one can be born [there]. Second, there is doubt that the Sahā world is ten trillion lands away from the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
how can it be so extremely distant, and yet one attains birth there? Third, even if one believes it is not far, there is doubt that ordinary beings have deep transgressions and heavy obstructions;

how can they suddenly attain birth in that land? Fourth, even if one believes they can be born there, there is doubt that being born in this Pure Land must necessarily involve planting many roots of merit.
Regarding merit: why is it that by merely upholding the name, one can attain rebirth in the Pure Land?

Furthermore, even if one believes in and upholds the name, one may still doubt that upholding this name will only achieve fulfillment after passing through many kalpas; how then can it be accomplished in a single day or seven days?

Thus one attains birth there; this is the sixth point. Even if one believes that birth is attained after seven days, yet one still doubts whether birth within the seven realms of existence does not involve the four modes of birth—namely, womb, egg, moisture, or transformation—how can it be so in that land?
This is the seventh point: [the answer is] that all therein are born from lotus flowers. Even if one believes they are born from lotuses, [one may still wonder...]
Furthermore, there is doubt that those who first enter the Way encounter many conditions for regression; how then can they attain non-regression upon being born in that land?

This is the eighth [doubt]. Even if one believes in non-regression, there is further doubt regarding the reception of sentient beings with dull faculties, as well as those of superior wisdom and sharp roots.
It is not necessary that one must be born in those nine [realms]. Even those with sharp faculties who possess faith may be born there.

Furthermore, they doubt other sutras—some say there is a Buddha, while others say there is no Buddha; some say there is a Pure Land, while others say there is no Pure Land. Thus, it is difficult to believe.
When it says "all worlds," this refers not only to the difficulty of belief among those in the evil realms, but also to humans and devas who may harbor such doubts. It is not only...

It is difficult for the ignorant and deluded to believe; yet even the wise and virtuous may harbor doubts. It is not only those of initial capacity who find it hard to believe, but even those of long-standing cultivation may doubt it.
It is not only ordinary beings who find it hard to believe, but even those of the Two Vehicles may harbor doubts. Now, in this world...
To expound this Dharma is the inconceivable merit of benefiting others. All of the above are the words of the Buddhas praising Śākyamuni.
Śāriputra, you should know that in this world of the five turbidities and evil ages, I have performed this difficult task and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
To preach this dharma so difficult to believe for the sake of all the worlds—this is most difficult.

This is a reiteration of the words of all Buddhas to clarify the matter. Seeing these two difficulties, one sees that the ancient Buddhas did not praise it in vain, and the present Buddha does not unwarrantedly receive such glorious renown. There are two difficulties regarding the attainment of the Way; the first is said to be goodness...
To attain the Way in a world of peace is not difficult. Now, in this evil age—to attain the Way and yet achieve only a minor fruit—is still not difficult.
But to now attain unsurpassed *bodhi* is what makes it difficult. There are likewise two difficulties regarding the preaching of the Dharma:
first, preaching the Dharma in a world of peace is not difficult; second, [preaching] now in this evil age.

To preach the Dharma in an evil age while those who are easily led have faith is not yet considered difficult; but now, to preach this Dharma that is difficult to believe—this is what makes it difficult.
The Tathāgata did not shrink from toil, having endured every hardship for our sake, performing the most difficult of difficulties to such an extent as this.
Upon hearing of this difficulty, all should experience a mingling of joy and sorrow, moved to deep emotion.
Tears fall. With courageous and diligent effort, one should contemplate repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
Section Twelve: The Distribution for Universal Salvation.

[The Buddha] raised his voice for the assembly to listen. Second, they received it with faith and practiced accordingly.
