He recited this prayer incessantly. At dawn, the prisoners were released; their shackles and fetters were removed. When it came to three men, the instruments of punishment were insufficient, so they were bound only with ropes.
Subsequently, upon interrogation, it was discovered that these were commoners who had been abducted, and they were thus set free.
Zhang Shanhe of the Tang dynasty made his living as a butcher of oxen. As he approached the end of his life, he saw a herd of oxen coming to claim his life.
Stricken with great terror, he called to his wife, saying, "Quickly invite a monk to recite the Buddha’s name for me.

When the monk arrived, he instructed him, saying, "If such evil omens appear at the moment of death, simply recite the Buddha’s name with a sincere heart, and you will attain rebirth in the Pure Land. Shanhe replied, "Hell is most urgent; I must fetch incense."
The incense burner arrived. He immediately held the fire with his right hand and grasped the incense with his left. Facing west, he recited the Buddha’s name with single-minded intensity.
Before ten recitations were completed, he said of himself, "The Buddha has come to welcome me," and he immediately passed away.
Master Guan of Zhengdeng Monastery in Huangyan, Song, kept a myna bird that constantly recited the Buddha’s name without ceasing.
One day, it passed away while standing atop its cage. Master Guan buried it, and subsequently, a single purple lotus emerged from the earth, sprouting from the tip of its tongue.
Dharma Master Zhaolinyi of Lingzhi composed a verse in praise of this: "To die standing upon the closed cage is but a trivial matter; The transformation [of the lotus]..."
The "Purple Lotus" is an exceedingly marvelous verse.
Attached herein are the essential sayings of Great Master Yufeng,
transcribed with blood.
The Teacher of the Sahā world, while at the assembly in the Jeta Grove, preached one fascicle of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
The Buddhas of the six directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, praised it with one voice and protected it with their mindful attention.

Furthermore, he extended his broad and long tongue, covering the entire great trichiliocosm, and universally exhorted all sentient beings that they should believe and accept it. Why is this? It is because this sutra directly reveals the [Buddha-nature] of all beings.

This is because it thoroughly fulfills the fundamental intention of all Buddhas to universally deliver sentient beings who have long been mired in delusion regarding their own nature. Thus, a sutra states:
"When the future teachings and Dharma are extinguished, this sutra alone shall remain for a hundred years. Should sentient beings encounter it, they shall all attain liberation."
If there are sentient beings who hear this sutra, they shall never regress from the unsurpassed path.

For this reason, one should single-mindedly believe and accept it, upholding, reciting, explaining, and practicing it. Gu Kun has composed these ritual procedures for visualization and offering as a daily practice.
I wished once more to propagate this sutra widely for the sake of others to repay the Buddha’s kindness; yet, with a dull tongue and a clouded mind, I am unable to fulfill my vow.

How could I not feel the utmost regret? My obstacles are deep and my merit is meager, reaching such a state as this. I reflect that had I remained a layperson, I would never have encountered this sutra, and thus I certainly could not have resolved to leave the household life.
Had I left the household life without relying upon this sutra, I certainly could not have brought forth a death-defying resolve to contemplate it.
"Buddha, this kindness and this virtue are difficult to repay and difficult to requite. For this reason, I have often thought of drawing blood to transcribe this sutra as an offering to you.

Yet, ashamed of my lack of fortitude, I did not dare to begin. It was not until the Guiyou year of the Tongzhi era that I suddenly contracted a disease of the tongue which did not subside after a long time;
this must surely be the retribution for the false speech of my past lives. If I do not repent, I shall certainly fall into the three [evil realms]."
Thereupon, he gave rise to a resolute mind. Before an image of Śākyamuni, he respectfully pierced his tongue to draw blood and transcribed the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

Furthermore, he burned nine incense sticks from his arm as an offering to the Teacher of the Sahā World, our Original Master Śākyamuni Buddha, Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and all the Buddhas of the six directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. He then made this vow:
The Vow states: This disciple, Gu Kun, has observed that within the sutras it is said: "If one has already made a vow, one will be born [in that state];
if one makes a vow now, one will be born [there] now; if one shall make a vow, one shall be born [there] in the future. Therefore, I now make this vow with a sincere heart.
I have contracted a tongue ailment difficult to eradicate; it must surely stem from much false speech throughout many lifetimes.
To manifest my utmost sincerity, I write out the *Amitābha Sūtra* using blood drawn from my own tongue.
By means of this virtuous cause of drawing blood, may I repent for and eliminate all evil karma of the tongue-root.
May I, at the time when my life is about to end, Certainly attain entry into the lower-grade lotus;
I pray only that this lotus may quickly open, That I may soon obtain the Tathāgata’s broad and long tongue,
And vow to enter this evil world of Sahā To minutely explain this wondrous sutra.
Appearing in response to sounds as wondrous adornments, May all who see or hear be filled with joy;
May every person recite the name of Amitābha, And each and every one be born together in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
I reverently pray that the Buddha there, our Original Teacher, And the Buddhas of the six directions mentioned in this sutra, [May they all grant their protection and blessings.]
May Great Compassion and Great Mercy likewise bear witness: may my vows be thus without rest, directly manifesting the ultimate. The *Yuanzhong chao* states:
"The jade groves and gemstone ponds directly manifest the source of the mind; the lifespan and radiance fully reveal one's own nature (*svabhāva*).
By merely citing a provisional name, all actual phenomena are fully encompassed; therefore, it is called 'One Utterance is Auspicious'."
The Name: The myriad virtues are simultaneously manifested. This means that one practices according to this sutra simply by taking the six-syllable sound of the Buddha’s name as the object of focus.
One does not employ the contemplation of the Buddha’s physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), lest it confuse the essential tenet of the scripture.
The *Yaojie* (Essential Explanation) states: "Amitābha Buddha is the great name of the myriad virtues; when virtue is summoned by means of the name, nothing remains unexhausted."
Therefore, simply holding the name constitutes the primary practice; there is no need to further engage in practices such as visualization or investigative inquiry.
This is most simple and most direct. Thus, Che-wu said: "The Buddha who is the object of this single phrase is established by name based on his complete virtues.
There is no name apart from virtue, for virtue is summoned by the name. There is no virtue apart from the name, for it is fundamentally pervasive throughout all things."
This essence contains all things; it is absolute, perfectly interfused, and inconceivable. Practitioners of the Lotus School should enter through faith from this very point.

It is further said: "With deep faith and earnest vows, holding the Name with single-minded sincerity, one can, in every thought-moment, purify all defilements, fully manifest original emptiness, suddenly accord with the spiritual source, and proceed directly toward the ocean of fruition. This is the sequence of the path.
That is to say: a single phrase of Amitābha cuts across the source of delusion and plunges directly into the ocean of awakening;

it is the most simple, easy, direct, and expedient of great skillful means. As evidenced by the citations above, these all represent the principle of direct manifestation. May those who hold to the Name take this to heart.
They were equally devoted in their efforts.

I once saw a student who possessed a "Praise of the Buddha-land" (Fo-tu song) and a single fascicle of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, both of which he claimed explained that everything is the inherent nature of one's own mind, and that there is no such thing as [a separate] "there."
"To seek the Buddha in that land is it not to deny the object while searching for the mind? It is like cutting off one's own head to look for life.
When Kun heard this, he could not bear it and thus composed the "Verses on the Existence of Buddha-Lands" to admonish the ignorant.
How great is this single scroll of the Shorter Amitābha Sūtra! The character "Buddha" alone accounts for eighty-five strokes; yet, one sees only the Three Minds within it.
How could one dare say there is no Buddha? Would that not be a grave offense?

Seeking the character "Earth" (土), twenty-one [instances] are found; searching everywhere for the character "Nature" (性), no trace remains. Clearly, the presence of "Earth" is the Perfect Teaching (圓談);
it does not compare to the Lesser Vehicle (小乘), which speaks mostly of quiescence.

Chanting the name for self-comfort—I call upon the Buddha. These are not the same. It is entirely through the deluded mind that great efficacy is revealed. In times of peace, who knows the power of the army?
Only when the bandit arrives does one see the majesty of the general.
Empty delusions are as chaotic as tangled threads; how could one know them without mindfulness of Amitābha? When the mirror of the mind is first polished, all reflections appear;
one should know that the Buddha’s name is wondrous and inconceivable.

Reciting the Buddha’s name and using the prayer beads to count—transforming the ordinary into the sacred, its merit is difficult to measure. If you wish to seek the Land of Ultimate Bliss and swiftly transcend this life, it requires nothing more than counting daily without confusion.

When the mouth recites the Buddha’s name, the mind will surely become pure. It is like a person suffering from a severe nightmare who hears a voice calling out; because of this, they no longer fear the many disturbances of the mind, but only fear that the sound of the Buddha’s name may cease from their mouth.
In the "Preface to the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation" by the First Patriarch of the Lotus School, it is said:

"Now, when the profound resonance strikes, worldly burdens are constantly dissolved and obstructed emotions are clarified; were it not for the ultimate subtlety of this world, who could participate in this?
This is why I, Gu Kun, always urge those who uphold the Name never to fear discursive thoughts or loathe their karmic defilements, but rather to first seek single-mindedness."
Do not let [the mind] be distracted; simply utter the sound and count. Make the end of life your limit. Each time the Buddha utters a sound, the bead is counted once;
thus, worldly burdens are constantly dissolved and obstructive emotions are clarified and brightened. The merit becomes ever more sublime. As the Sūtra says: "In every moment of thought..."
It eliminates the offenses of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas; thus, worldly burdens are gradually dissolved. It is further said:
"If one recites even a single name with a distracted mind, one has already attained the Way of Buddhahood. Thus, obstructive emotions are harmonized and clarified.

How could it be that delusive thoughts are not lightened from time to time, and karmic defilements not diminished from time to time? With each utterance of the Buddha’s name, there is a resonance; with every sound, there is the Buddha.

"Each sound corresponds with the next"—is this not precisely what is meant? You should know that as you recite the name and keep count, making the end of your life your deadline, even if you have not yet reached the state of "single-mindedness without distraction," your faith and vow will surely become firm and steadfast, and rebirth in the Pure Land can certainly be expected.

It is merely that one’s level of attainment is temporarily low. Thus, the essential explanation states: whether or not one attains birth [in the Pure Land] depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and aspiration;
the high or low level of one’s attainment depends entirely on the depth of one’s recitation of the Name. I inform all those with the karmic affinity:
during the time of recitation, it is sufficient simply to ensure that the sound does not cease; there is no need to fixate on "single-mindedness."
Chaos. Uninterrupted sound is the cause; single-mindedness without confusion is the fruit. If the causal practice is genuine, the fruit will surely be accomplished—of itself and naturally.
As the saying goes: "When the form is straight, the shadow is upright; when the sound is harmonious, the echo is compliant.
It is a pity that people of the present day do not even wish to recite it constantly. Within every phrase, there is the power to dissolve the dust of afflictions and melt away all stagnation.
Furthermore, they do not know its merits. Thus, they first imagine a state of single-mindedness without distraction;
is this not like a bird attempting to fly without wings, or a tree seeking to flourish without roots? Consequently, every time they recite the name of Amitābha, it lacks flavor.
As their delusive thoughts increase, they turn toward other gates. Alas, how tragic! Is this not the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land?
To have declined to this extent may be called reaching the limit. I pray that those of my own school will exert themselves to produce the sound and keep count.
One must know that producing the sound pertains to the mouth, while keeping count pertains to the body. Thus, Chan Master Miaoye said:

"If one can direct the mindfulness of both body and mouth, do not concern oneself with whether it is scattered; provided it is not interrupted, one will naturally attain single-mindedness. This is also acceptable.
This is precisely what is called "single-mindedness. One simply practices it without ceasing; this constitutes deliverance. There is truly no need to worry about mental distraction.

It is like a mother who has lost her beloved child, or a dragon who has lost its life-giving pearl: the mind becomes one not by expectation, but spontaneously. How could it be that one forces it to become one?
That the mind cannot be forcibly constrained depends entirely upon whether the practitioner is diligent or indolent.
